lessons.title: Rates of Reaction and Collision Theory

before.content_html:
What Is Rate of Reaction?

The rate of reaction tells us how fast a chemical reaction happens. Some reactions are very fast — like an explosion or the neutralisation of an acid. Others are very slow, such as rusting or the weathering of rocks. In GCSE Chemistry, you need to know how to measure, calculate, and explain what controls the rate of a reaction.

Rate of reaction can be defined as the amount of product formed, or the amount of reactant used up, per unit of time. The equation is:

Key Fact

\(Rate \text{of reaction} = \text{amount of product formed} \div time\) — or — \(\text{amount of reactant used up} \div time\). The units depend on what you measure: g/s if you measure mass, or cm³/s if you measure the volume of gas produced.

Measuring Rate of Reaction

There are two main practical methods for measuring rate of reaction at GCSE. Both appear in the AQA required practicals and you need to know the advantages and limitations of each.

When a reaction produces a gas, you can collect and measure the gas using a gas syringe or by collecting the gas over water using an inverted measuring cylinder. You record the volume of gas at regular time intervals (e.g. every 10 seconds) and plot a graph of volume against time.

Example: Marble chips (calcium carbonate) reacting with hydrochloric acid: CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2. The carbon dioxide gas is collected in the gas syringe. The faster the syringe plunger moves out, the faster the reaction.

Place the reaction flask on a balance and record the mass at regular time intervals. As gas escapes from the flask, the mass decreases. You plot a graph of mass lost against time. This method works well for reactions that produce carbon dioxide or hydrogen gas.

Advantage: Easy to set up and gives continuous data. Disadvantage: Gas escapes into the room, so the mass readings are slightly less accurate than collecting the gas directly. Very light gases like hydrogen are hard to detect by mass loss.

Reading Rate from a Graph

When you plot a graph of product formed (or reactant used up) against time, the gradient (steepness) of the line tells you the rate. A steep line means a fast reaction. A shallow line means a slow reaction. When the line goes flat, the reaction has finished — one of the reactants has been completely used up.

To calculate the rate at a specific point on a curved graph, draw a tangent to the curve at that point and find the gradient of the tangent. The gradient equals the change in the y-axis divided by the change in the x-axis.

Key Fact

\(Gradient = \text{change in} y \div \text{change in} x.\) On a volume–time graph, this gives rate in cm³/s. On a mass-loss graph, it gives rate in g/s. The mean rate for the whole reaction is the total product formed divided by the total time taken.

Collision Theory

Collision theory explains why reactions happen at different rates. For a reaction to occur, the reacting particles must collide with each other. But not every collision leads to a reaction — two conditions must be met:

1. The particles must collide with enough energy. The minimum energy needed for a collision to result in a reaction is called the activation energy. If particles collide with less energy than this, they just bounce apart. 2. The particles must collide in the correct orientation — they need to hit each other the right way round so that bonds can break and new bonds can form.

Anything that increases the frequency of successful collisions will increase the rate of reaction. The four main factors that do this are temperature, concentration, surface area, and catalysts.

Factors Affecting Rate

Temperature

Increasing the temperature makes particles move faster because they have more kinetic energy. This has two effects: particles collide more often (higher collision frequency), and a greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy. Both effects increase the rate. This is why reactions are usually faster when heated.

Concentration (and Pressure for Gases)

Increasing the concentration of a solution means there are more reactant particles in the same volume. This increases the frequency of collisions, so the rate increases. For gaseous reactions, increasing the pressure has the same effect — it forces particles closer together so they collide more often.

Surface Area

Breaking a solid into smaller pieces increases its surface area. More surface is exposed to the other reactant, so more collisions can happen at the same time. For example, powdered marble chips react much faster with hydrochloric acid than large lumps because the powder has a much greater surface area.

Key Fact

All four factors — temperature, concentration, surface area, and catalysts — affect rate by changing the frequency or energy of collisions. In every exam answer, link back to collision theory: more frequent collisions or more energetic collisions means a faster rate.

Catalysts

A catalyst is a substance that increases the rate of a reaction without being used up. It works by providing an alternative reaction pathway that has a lower activation energy. This means a greater proportion of collisions now have enough energy to react, so the rate increases. The catalyst is chemically unchanged at the end — it can be reused.

Enzymes are biological catalysts that control reactions in living organisms. In industry, catalysts are used to reduce energy costs — reactions can run at lower temperatures, saving fuel and money. Different reactions require different catalysts.

AQA’s required practical investigates how changing one factor (e.g. concentration of acid or size of marble chips) affects the rate of reaction between marble chips and dilute hydrochloric acid. You measure the volume of CO2 produced using a gas syringe and record it at regular intervals.

Key points: Use the same mass of marble chips and the same volume of acid each time (control variables). Change only the independent variable (e.g. concentration). Repeat each test at least three times and calculate a mean. Plot the results on a graph — steeper curves mean faster reactions.

Common error: Students often forget that although the rate changes, the total volume of gas produced stays the same (when excess acid is used) because the same mass of marble chips is always used. The reaction just finishes sooner at higher concentrations or temperatures.

When two curves are plotted on the same axes, the steeper curve represents the faster reaction. If both curves reach the same final volume, the same amount of reactant was used — the reaction just finished sooner. If one curve reaches a lower final volume, less gas was produced (e.g. less reactant was used). Be ready to explain these differences using collision theory.

What Is a Reversible Reaction?

Most chemical reactions you have studied so far go in one direction — reactants turn into products and the reaction stops. But some reactions can go in both directions. In a reversible reaction, the products can react to reform the original reactants. We show this using the equilibrium symbol ⇌ instead of a normal arrow.

A classic example is the thermal decomposition of ammonium chloride. When heated, ammonium chloride (a white solid) breaks down into ammonia and hydrogen chloride — two colourless gases. When these gases cool and meet, they recombine to form ammonium chloride again:

\(\text{ammonium chloride} \rightleftharpoons ammonia + \text{hydrogen chloride}\)
NH4Cl(s) ⇌ NH3(g) + HCl(g)

You can see this in action: when you heat ammonium chloride in a test tube, a white solid forms higher up in the tube where the gases have cooled and recombined. This proves the reaction is reversible.

Key Fact

The ⇌ symbol tells you a reaction is reversible. A normal arrow (→) means the reaction only goes one way. Never use a normal arrow for a reversible reaction in the exam.

Hydrated Copper Sulfate — Another Reversible Reaction

Another important example is the hydration of copper sulfate. Hydrated copper sulfate is a blue crystalline solid. When you heat it, it loses its water of crystallisation and turns into a white powder called anhydrous copper sulfate:

\(\text{hydrated copper sulfate} (blue) \rightleftharpoons \text{anhydrous copper sulfate} (white) + water\)
CuSO4·5H2O(s) ⇌ CuSO4(s) + 5H2O(l)

If you add water back to the white anhydrous powder, it turns blue again and gets hot — the reverse reaction is exothermic. This colour change is so reliable that anhydrous copper sulfate is used as a chemical test for the presence of water.

To test for the presence of water, add the liquid to white anhydrous copper sulfate. If the powder turns blue, water is present. This does not tell you the water is pure — to confirm pure water, check the boiling point (100 °C at standard pressure). Cobalt chloride paper can also be used: it turns from blue to pink when water is present.

Energy Changes in Reversible Reactions

In any reversible reaction, if the forward reaction is exothermic (gives out energy), then the reverse reaction is endothermic (takes in energy) — and vice versa. The amount of energy transferred in each direction is exactly the same.

For the copper sulfate example: the forward reaction (heating blue copper sulfate to drive off water) is endothermic — you have to supply heat energy. The reverse reaction (adding water to the white powder) is exothermic — the mixture gets hot. The energy released going one way equals the energy absorbed going the other way.

Key Fact

If a reversible reaction is exothermic in the forward direction, it is endothermic in the reverse direction — and the energy change is the same in both directions. This is a common exam question.

Dynamic Equilibrium

When a reversible reaction takes place in a closed system (where nothing can get in or out), something interesting happens. At first the forward reaction is fast because there are lots of reactants. As products build up, the reverse reaction speeds up. Eventually, the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction. This is called dynamic equilibrium.

“Dynamic” means that both reactions are still happening — molecules are constantly reacting in both directions. “Equilibrium” means the overall concentrations of reactants and products stay the same because the two rates are balanced. It is not a static situation where everything has stopped.

Key Fact

Dynamic equilibrium requires a closed system. The forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so concentrations of reactants and products do not change — but the reaction has not stopped.

Le Châtelier’s Principle

Le Châtelier’s principle states that if a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change in conditions, the position of equilibrium shifts to partially oppose that change. In other words, the system tries to “undo” whatever you did to it. This principle lets you predict which way the equilibrium will shift when you change temperature, pressure, or concentration.

If you increase the temperature, the equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction to absorb the extra heat. If you decrease the temperature, the equilibrium shifts in the exothermic direction to release heat and restore the temperature. Changing temperature changes both the rate and the position of equilibrium — and therefore changes the yield of products.

Example: In a reversible reaction where the forward reaction is exothermic, increasing the temperature will favour the reverse (endothermic) reaction, producing more reactants and fewer products. The yield of products decreases.

For reactions involving gases, changing the pressure affects the equilibrium position. If you increase the pressure, the equilibrium shifts towards the side with fewer moles of gas — this reduces the pressure. If you decrease the pressure, the equilibrium shifts towards the side with more moles of gas.

Example: Consider N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g). The left side has 4 moles of gas (1 + 3) and the right side has 2. Increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right, producing more ammonia.

If you increase the concentration of a reactant, the equilibrium shifts to the right (forward direction) to use up the extra reactant, producing more products. If you increase the concentration of a product, the equilibrium shifts to the left (reverse direction) to use up the extra product.

Example: In the reaction A + B ⇌ C + D, adding more of substance A shifts the equilibrium to the right, increasing the yield of C and D until a new equilibrium is established.

Catalysts and Equilibrium

A catalyst speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally. This means a catalyst helps the system reach equilibrium faster, but it does not change the position of equilibrium or the yield of products. The same amounts of reactants and products are present at equilibrium whether a catalyst is used or not — you just get there more quickly.

Applying Equilibrium: The Haber Process

The Haber process is a real-world application of equilibrium principles. Nitrogen from the air reacts with hydrogen (from natural gas) to produce ammonia:

\(N_{2}(g) + 3H_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_{3}(g)\) — the forward reaction is exothermic.

Using Le Châtelier’s principle: a low temperature and high pressure would give the best yield of ammonia. However, low temperatures make the reaction too slow, so a compromise temperature of about 450 °C is used. High pressure (around 200 atmospheres) favours ammonia production. An iron catalyst is used to speed up the reaction without changing the yield. Any unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled back through the reactor.

Key Fact

The Haber process uses a compromise temperature (about 450 °C), high pressure (200 atm), and an iron catalyst. High pressure increases yield; the moderate temperature balances acceptable yield with a reasonable rate of reaction.

lessons.title: Chemical Analysis: Purity, Chromatography and Gas Tests

before.content_html:
Pure Substances in Chemistry

In everyday language, “pure” means natural or uncontaminated — like “pure orange juice.” But in chemistry, the word has a very specific meaning. A pure substance contains only a single element or a single compound. Pure water, for example, contains nothing but H2O molecules. Crude oil is not pure because it is a mixture of many different hydrocarbons.

Key Fact

A pure substance has a sharp melting point and a sharp boiling point. An impure substance melts and boils over a range of temperatures. Impurities lower the melting point and raise the boiling point. For example, pure water melts at exactly 0°C and boils at exactly 100°C, but seawater (which contains dissolved salt) melts below 0°C.

This means that if you measure the melting point of an unknown white powder and find it melts sharply at one temperature, it is likely pure. If it melts gradually over a range of temperatures, it is a mixture.

Formulations

A formulation is a special type of mixture. The components are mixed in carefully measured quantities so that the final product has exactly the right properties for its purpose. Unlike a random mixture, each ingredient in a formulation serves a specific function.

Formulations are everywhere in daily life. Medicines contain an active ingredient plus binders, coatings, and flavourings. Paints are formulations of pigment, solvent, binder, and additives. Other examples include cleaning products, fuels, cosmetics, fertilisers, and alloys. Each component is present in a precise proportion — too much or too little of any ingredient would change the product’s properties.

Medicine: A paracetamol tablet contains the active drug (paracetamol) plus binding agents that hold the tablet together, a coating for easy swallowing, and sometimes flavouring. The exact mass of each component is critical — too much active ingredient could be dangerous.

Paint: Contains a pigment (for colour), a solvent (to keep it liquid), a binder (to make it stick to surfaces), and additives (to control drying time or finish). Changing the proportions changes whether the paint is matt or gloss, fast-drying or slow-drying.

Chromatography

Chromatography is a powerful analytical technique used to separate mixtures of soluble substances. It can reveal whether a substance is pure or impure, and it can identify the individual components of a mixture.

Paper chromatography involves two phases. The mobile phase is the solvent (often water) that moves up through the paper. The stationary phase is the paper itself. Different substances in the mixture are carried different distances by the solvent, depending on how soluble they are. More soluble substances travel further up the paper; less soluble ones stay closer to the start line.

Step 1: Draw a pencil line 1 cm from the bottom of the chromatography paper. Use pencil, not pen, because pencil ink is insoluble and will not dissolve in the solvent.

Step 2: Place small spots of each substance onto the pencil line, leaving gaps between them so they do not merge.

Step 3: Pour a shallow layer of solvent into a beaker. The solvent level must be below the pencil line so that the spots do not dissolve directly into the solvent.

Step 4: Lower the paper into the solvent and leave it undisturbed. The solvent will travel up the paper by capillary action, carrying the dissolved substances with it.

Step 5: Remove the paper just before the solvent front reaches the top. Mark the solvent front with a pencil and allow the chromatogram to dry.

Interpreting a Chromatogram

The pattern of spots on a finished chromatogram tells you important information. A pure substance produces just one spot. An impure substance (a mixture) produces two or more spots, one for each component in the mixture.

You can identify unknown substances by comparing their spots to known reference substances run on the same chromatogram. If an unknown spot travels the same distance as a known substance, they are likely the same chemical.

Calculating Rf Values

The Rf value (retention factor) gives each substance a numerical identity in a particular solvent. It is calculated using:

Key Fact

\(R_{f} = \text{distance moved by substance} \div \text{distance moved by solvent}\). The Rf value is always between 0 and 1. Each substance has a unique Rf value in a given solvent, so Rf values can be compared to reference data to identify unknown chemicals.

Worked example: A spot of dye travels 30 mm up the paper. The solvent front travels 52 mm. Rf = 30 ÷ 52 = 0.58 (to 2 significant figures). Different compounds have different Rf values in different solvents, so the solvent used and the conditions must always be recorded.

Tests for Common Gases

You need to know the laboratory tests for four gases: hydrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide, and chlorine. Each test has a specific method and a clear positive result that you must be able to recall.

Hydrogen: Hold a burning splint at the mouth of a test tube containing the gas. If hydrogen is present, it burns rapidly with a squeaky pop sound. Hydrogen is produced when metals react with acids (e.g. magnesium + hydrochloric acid).

Oxygen: Insert a glowing splint into a test tube of the gas. If oxygen is present, the splint relights. Oxygen can be produced by decomposing hydrogen peroxide with a manganese dioxide catalyst.

Carbon dioxide: Bubble the gas through limewater (calcium hydroxide solution). If carbon dioxide is present, the limewater turns cloudy (milky white). This happens because calcium carbonate, an insoluble white solid, is formed. Carbon dioxide is produced when carbonates react with acids.

Chlorine: Hold a piece of damp litmus paper near the gas. If chlorine is present, the litmus paper is bleached white. This happens because chlorine dissolves in the water on the damp paper and acts as a bleaching agent.

Key Fact

Remember the four gas tests: Hydrogen → squeaky pop with a burning splint. Oxygen → relights a glowing splint. Carbon dioxide → turns limewater cloudy. Chlorine → bleaches damp litmus paper white.

Students often confuse the hydrogen and oxygen tests. For hydrogen, the splint must be burning (lit). For oxygen, the splint must be glowing (no flame, just an ember). Saying “the splint relights” when testing for hydrogen, or “a squeaky pop” when testing for oxygen, will lose you marks.

Another common error is stating that carbon dioxide “extinguishes a flame.” While this is true, it is not the correct test — many gases will extinguish a flame. The specific test is the limewater test. Similarly, for chlorine, the litmus paper must be damp, not dry.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a ‘pure substance’ in chemistry.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark(s) for:
• A substance that contains only one element or one compound (1)

Accept: a substance made of only one type of element or compound. Do not accept everyday definitions such as ‘nothing added to it’ without reference to elements or compounds.

practice_questions.text: Describe the test you would carry out to determine whether a sample of water is pure or impure.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Measure the melting point / boiling point of the sample (1)
• If pure, it will melt/boil at a single fixed temperature (e.g. 0°C / 100°C) / if impure, it will melt/boil over a range of temperatures (1)

Accept references to impurities lowering the melting point or raising the boiling point for the second mark.

practice_questions.text: A student carries out chromatography on a food dye. The dye travels 24 mm up the paper. The solvent front travels 60 mm. Calculate the R₆ value of the dye.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• R₆ = 24 ÷ 60 (1)
• = 0.40 (1)

Allow ecf if the formula is correctly applied to incorrect values. The correct answer alone scores both marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain how paper chromatography can be used to determine whether a sample of ink is a pure substance or a mixture.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• The ink is spotted onto a pencil line on chromatography paper and a solvent is allowed to travel up the paper (1)
• A pure substance will produce only one spot on the chromatogram (1)
• A mixture will produce two or more spots because it contains different substances that travel different distances / have different solubilities (1)

Accept references to comparing R₆ values with known substances for identification.

practice_questions.text: A student tests two unknown gases, Gas A and Gas B. Gas A produces a squeaky pop when a burning splint is placed at the mouth of the test tube. Gas B turns limewater cloudy when bubbled through it. Compare and explain the identity of each gas and the chemistry behind each test.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Gas A is hydrogen (1)
• The squeaky pop occurs because hydrogen burns / reacts rapidly with oxygen in the air (1)
• Gas B is carbon dioxide (1)
• Carbon dioxide reacts with the calcium hydroxide (limewater) to form calcium carbonate, which is an insoluble white precipitate that makes the solution look cloudy (1)

Accept word equation: calcium hydroxide + carbon dioxide → calcium carbonate + water for the fourth mark.

practice_questions.text: Formulations are important in many industries. Explain what is meant by a formulation and discuss why precise proportions of each component are important. Use examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed explanation of what a formulation is, with clear examples and a well-developed discussion of why precise proportions matter. Uses correct scientific terminology throughout.
Indicative content:
• A formulation is a mixture that has been designed as a useful product (1)
• Components are mixed in carefully measured / precise quantities (1)
• Each component has a specific function / purpose (1)
• Example: medicine contains active ingredient + binder + coating + flavouring (1)
• Example: paint contains pigment + solvent + binder + additives (1)
• If proportions are wrong, the product will not work correctly / could be dangerous (e.g. too much active drug) (1)
• Other examples: fuels, fertilisers, cleaning products, cosmetics, alloys (1)
• A formulation is different from a random mixture because it is designed for a specific function (1)
Mid band (3-4): Correct definition and at least one example, but limited discussion of why proportions matter.
Lower band (1-2): Basic definition of a formulation or a list of examples with no explanation.

before.content_html:
What Are Atmospheric Pollutants?

When we burn fossil fuels such as coal, oil and natural gas, they don’t just produce carbon dioxide and water. Depending on the conditions and the fuel itself, a range of harmful pollutants can be released into the atmosphere. These pollutants cause serious problems for human health and the environment.

The main atmospheric pollutants you need to know are carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and particulates. Each one is produced in a different way and causes different types of damage.

Key Fact

The four atmospheric pollutants you must know for AQA are: carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2), nitrogen oxides (NOx) and particulates (soot and unburnt hydrocarbons).

Complete and Incomplete Combustion

To understand where pollutants come from, you first need to understand the difference between complete combustion and incomplete combustion.

In complete combustion, a hydrocarbon fuel burns in a plentiful supply of oxygen. The only products are carbon dioxide and water. For example, methane burning completely:

\(methane + oxygen \rightarrow \text{carbon dioxide} + water\)
CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O

In incomplete combustion, there is not enough oxygen for the fuel to burn fully. Instead of carbon dioxide, the products include carbon monoxide (CO) and particulate carbon (soot). This is what happens inside a Bunsen burner when the air hole is closed — you see a yellow, smoky flame because carbon particles glow in the heat.

\(methane + oxygen \rightarrow \text{carbon monoxide} + water\)
2CH4 + 3O2 → 2CO + 4H2O

If even less oxygen is available, solid carbon (soot) is produced as well:

\(methane + oxygen \rightarrow carbon + water\)
CH4 + O2 → C + 2H2O

Incomplete combustion occurs when there is a limited supply of oxygen. This commonly happens in car engines (especially diesel engines), gas boilers that are poorly maintained, and any enclosed space where air flow is restricted. The larger the hydrocarbon molecule, the more oxygen it needs to burn completely — which is why diesel fuel (with bigger molecules than petrol) is more likely to undergo incomplete combustion and produce particulates.

Carbon Monoxide (CO)

carbon monoxide is a colourless, odourless gas, which makes it extremely dangerous because you cannot detect it without a special alarm. It is produced by the incomplete combustion of any fuel containing carbon.

Carbon monoxide is toxic because it binds to the haemoglobin in red blood cells. Haemoglobin normally carries oxygen from the lungs to the body’s tissues. Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen does, so it takes the place of oxygen molecules. This means less oxygen is carried around the body, which can lead to dizziness, unconsciousness and even death at high concentrations.

Key Fact

Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it is colourless and odourless, and it binds to haemoglobin in red blood cells, reducing the amount of oxygen the blood can carry.

Sulfur Dioxide (SO2)

sulfur dioxide is produced when fossil fuels that contain sulfur impurities are burned. Coal is particularly high in sulfur. The sulfur reacts with oxygen during combustion:

\(sulfur + oxygen \rightarrow \text{sulfur dioxide}\)
S + O2 → SO2

Sulfur dioxide can also be released naturally by volcanic eruptions. Once in the atmosphere, it dissolves in rainwater to form acid rain (sulfurous acid or sulfuric acid):

\(SO_{2} + H_{2}O \rightarrow H_{2}SO_{3}\) (sulfurous acid)

Acid rain causes widespread environmental damage. It corrodes limestone and marble buildings and statues because these are made of calcium carbonate, which reacts with acid. It kills trees by damaging their leaves and leaching minerals from the soil. It also lowers the pH of lakes and rivers, killing fish and other aquatic organisms. Acid rain can travel hundreds of kilometres from the source of the pollution, meaning one country’s emissions can damage another country’s environment.

Nitrogen Oxides (NOx)

nitrogen oxides (written as NOx) are formed when the temperature inside an engine or furnace is high enough for nitrogen and oxygen in the air to react together. This does not come from the fuel itself — it comes from the atmosphere. Car engines, aeroplane engines and power stations all produce nitrogen oxides.

Nitrogen oxides also occur naturally during lightning strikes, where the extreme heat forces nitrogen and oxygen molecules to combine. However, the vast majority of nitrogen oxides in the atmosphere come from vehicle engines.

Nitrogen oxides cause several problems. Like sulfur dioxide, they dissolve in rainwater to form acid rain. They can also trigger asthma attacks and other respiratory problems. In sunlight, nitrogen oxides react with other pollutants to form photochemical smog, which is a serious health hazard in cities.

Key Fact

Nitrogen oxides are not produced from the fuel — they form when nitrogen and oxygen from the air react at the very high temperatures inside engines. They cause acid rain, trigger asthma and contribute to smog.

Particulates

particulates are tiny solid particles released during incomplete combustion. They consist of carbon (soot) and unburnt hydrocarbons. Diesel engines are a major source because diesel molecules are larger than petrol molecules and need more oxygen to burn completely.

Particulates cause two main types of harm:

Health effects: Particulates are so small that they can penetrate deep into the lungs and even pass across cell membranes into the bloodstream. They worsen respiratory conditions like asthma and bronchitis, and long-term exposure may increase the risk of lung cancer and heart disease.

Environmental effects: When particulates travel high into the atmosphere, they reflect sunlight back into space before it reaches the Earth’s surface. This effect is called global dimming. Some scientists have suggested that global dimming may partially offset the warming effect of greenhouse gases, but it also reduces the light available for photosynthesis and can disrupt weather patterns.

Several methods can reduce the release of atmospheric pollutants. Catalytic converters in car exhausts convert carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides into less harmful carbon dioxide and nitrogen. Flue gas desulfurisation in power stations removes sulfur dioxide from waste gases before they leave the chimney. Using cleaner fuels (such as natural gas instead of coal) or renewable energy sources avoids producing these pollutants altogether. Regular maintenance of boilers and engines ensures more complete combustion, reducing carbon monoxide and particulate emissions.

Carbon monoxide (CO): From incomplete combustion. Colourless, odourless. Binds to haemoglobin, reducing oxygen transport in blood.

\(Sulfur dioxide (SO_{2}):\) From burning fuels containing sulfur. Causes acid rain, damages buildings and kills aquatic life.

\(Nitrogen oxides (NO_{x}):\) From high-temperature reactions of N2 and O2 in engines. Cause acid rain, trigger asthma, form smog.

Particulates: Soot and unburnt hydrocarbons from incomplete combustion. Cause respiratory disease and global dimming.

before.content_html:
What Are Polymers?

A polymer is a very large molecule formed when many small molecules called monomers bond together in a repeating pattern. The word “polymer” comes from the Greek for “many parts.” Polymers can be synthetic (made by humans) or naturally occurring. Everyday synthetic polymers include poly(ethene), PVC, and PTFE, while natural polymers include proteins, starch, and DNA.

The process of joining monomers together is called polymerisation. There are two main types of polymerisation you need to know for GCSE Chemistry: addition polymerisation and condensation polymerisation. Each works in a different way and produces a different type of polymer.

Addition Polymerisation

addition polymerisation occurs when many unsaturated monomer molecules (alkenes) join together. The carbon–carbon double bond (C=C) in each monomer “opens up,” allowing the monomers to link into a long chain. No other substance is produced — the only product is the polymer itself.

The simplest example is poly(ethene). Ethene (C₂H₄) is the monomer. Under high pressure and with a catalyst, thousands of ethene molecules open their double bonds and bond together to form a long-chain polymer. The repeating unit of poly(ethene) looks the same as the monomer but with single bonds on each side instead of a double bond.

Key Fact

In addition polymerisation, the only product is the polymer. No atoms are lost or gained — the polymer has the same empirical formula as the monomer. The letter n in the equation represents a very large number of monomer molecules joining together.

To show addition polymerisation in an equation, write n monomer molecules on the left with the C=C double bond shown. On the right, draw the repeating unit inside brackets with a single bond extending from each side of the bracket. Place n as a subscript outside the brackets. The key change: the double bond in the monomer becomes a single bond in the polymer.

Common examples include poly(propene) from propene, and poly(chloroethene) — better known as PVC — from chloroethene. In each case, identify the alkene monomer, open the double bond, and extend the chain. Exam questions often ask you to draw the repeating unit given the monomer, or to identify the monomer from the polymer.

Condensation Polymerisation

condensation polymerisation is different from addition polymerisation in two important ways. First, the monomers have two functional groups — one on each end of the molecule. Second, a small molecule (usually water) is released every time two monomers join together. This by-product is the reason it is called “condensation” polymerisation.

Condensation polymers include polyesters and polyamides. To form a polyester, a dicarboxylic acid reacts with a diol. The –COOH group on the acid reacts with the –OH group on the alcohol, forming an ester link (–COO–) and releasing a molecule of water (H₂O) each time.

Key Fact

The crucial difference: addition polymerisation produces only the polymer, while condensation polymerisation produces the polymer and a small molecule by-product (usually water). This is the most common comparison question in the exam.

A polyamide forms when a dicarboxylic acid reacts with a diamine. The –COOH group reacts with the –NH₂ group, forming an amide link (–CONH–) and releasing water. Nylon is a well-known synthetic polyamide.

amino acids are special monomers because each molecule contains both an amine group (–NH₂) and a carboxylic acid group (–COOH). This means amino acids can undergo condensation polymerisation with each other. When two amino acids join, a peptide bond forms (a type of amide link) and water is released. Chains of amino acids form polypeptides, and one or more polypeptides fold into a protein.

Naturally Occurring Polymers

Many of the most important molecules in living organisms are polymers. You need to know three key examples for the exam: proteins, starch, and DNA. Each is built from smaller monomer units through condensation polymerisation.

Proteins are natural polyamides. They are condensation polymers of amino acids linked by peptide bonds. There are 20 different amino acids found in nature, and the order in which they join determines the protein’s shape and function. Proteins act as enzymes, hormones, antibodies, and structural materials such as collagen and keratin.

starch is a natural polymer made from glucose monomers joined together by condensation reactions. Plants produce starch to store energy. Cellulose is another glucose-based polymer, but the glucose units are arranged differently, giving cellulose rigid, structural properties. Both starch and cellulose release water molecules when their monomers join.

DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a polymer made from nucleotide monomers. Each nucleotide contains a sugar, a phosphate group, and a base. Nucleotides join by condensation reactions to form the two strands of the DNA double helix. The sequence of bases along the strand carries the genetic instructions for building proteins.

Key Fact

All three naturally occurring polymers — proteins, starch, and DNA — are formed by condensation polymerisation. In every case, monomers join together and water molecules are released as by-products.

Comparing the Two Types of Polymerisation

Exam questions frequently ask you to compare addition and condensation polymerisation. The table below summarises the key differences.

Addition polymerisation: monomers are alkenes with C=C double bonds; only one product (the polymer); no by-product; examples include poly(ethene), poly(propene), PVC. Condensation polymerisation: monomers have two functional groups (e.g. –OH and –COOH); two products (the polymer and a small molecule, usually water); examples include polyesters, nylon, proteins, starch, DNA.

Question: A polymer is formed from monomers with two different functional groups. Water is also produced. What type of polymerisation is this?

Answer: This is condensation polymerisation. The clues are: (1) the monomers have two functional groups, not a C=C double bond, and (2) a small molecule (water) is produced as a by-product. In addition polymerisation, there is no by-product — only the polymer is formed.

A small, reactive molecule that joins with others to form a polymer chain.
A chemical reaction in which many monomer molecules join together to form a polymer.
_____ (C₂H₄) is the monomer

flashcard_questions.a: A type of polymerisation in which unsaturated monomers (alkenes) open their double bonds and join together, producing only the polymer with no other product.

before.content_html:
Identifying Ions

In chemistry, you often need to identify which ions are present in an unknown substance. Ions are charged particles formed when atoms gain or lose electrons. Metal atoms lose electrons to form cations (positive ions), while non-metal atoms gain electrons to form anions (negative ions). There are reliable chemical tests for identifying both types, and you need to know them all for your exam.

Flame Tests

A flame test is used to identify certain metal ions. When compounds containing these metals are heated in a flame, the metal ions emit light of a characteristic colour. To carry out a flame test, you dip a clean nichrome wire loop into hydrochloric acid, then into the sample, and hold it in the blue flame of a Bunsen burner.

Key Fact

You must memorise these flame test colours: lithium — crimson, sodium — yellow, potassium — lilac, calcium — orange-red, copper — green. The wire must be cleaned with hydrochloric acid between tests to avoid contamination.

Lithium (Li¹⁺): Produces a crimson (deep red) flame. Lithium compounds are used in batteries and fireworks — the red colour in fireworks often comes from lithium salts.

Sodium (Na¹⁺): Produces a strong yellow flame. Sodium is so common as a contaminant that its yellow colour can mask other flame colours, which is why the wire must be thoroughly cleaned.

Potassium (K¹⁺): Produces a lilac (pale purple) flame. This can be hard to see if sodium is also present, as the yellow colour dominates.

\(Calcium (Ca^{2}⁺):\) Produces an orange-red flame. This is distinct from lithium’s crimson — calcium’s colour has more orange in it.

\(Copper (Cu^{2}⁺):\) Produces a green flame. Copper compounds are also responsible for the green colour in some fireworks.

Testing with Sodium Hydroxide Solution

Some metal ions cannot be identified by flame tests. Instead, you add a few drops of sodium hydroxide solution (NaOH) to a solution of the unknown compound. If certain metal ions are present, an insoluble metal hydroxide forms as a coloured precipitate.

Key Fact

Sodium hydroxide precipitate colours: aluminium — white (dissolves in excess NaOH), calcium — white (does not dissolve in excess), magnesium — white (does not dissolve in excess), copper(II) — blue, iron(II) — green, iron(III) — brown.

\(Aluminium ions (Al^{3}⁺):\) Form a white precipitate of aluminium hydroxide, Al(OH)3. Crucially, this precipitate dissolves when excess NaOH is added. This distinguishes aluminium from calcium and magnesium, which also give white precipitates but do not dissolve in excess.

\(Calcium ions (Ca^{2}⁺):\) Form a white precipitate of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)2. This does not dissolve in excess NaOH.

\(Magnesium ions (Mg^{2}⁺):\) Form a white precipitate of magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)2. This does not dissolve in excess NaOH. It is distinguished from calcium by flame test (calcium gives orange-red; magnesium gives no flame colour).

\(Copper(II) ions (Cu^{2}⁺):\) Form a blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide, Cu(OH)2.

\(Iron(II) ions (Fe^{2}⁺):\) Form a green precipitate of iron(II) hydroxide, Fe(OH)2. Sometimes called a “sludgy green” or “dirty green” colour.

\(Iron(III) ions (Fe^{3}⁺):\) Form a brown precipitate of iron(III) hydroxide, Fe(OH)3. This is a distinctive rusty brown colour.

Testing for Carbonate Ions

Carbonate ions (CO3²¯) are tested by adding dilute hydrochloric acid to the substance. If carbonates are present, the mixture fizzes and produces carbon dioxide gas. You confirm that the gas is carbon dioxide by passing it through limewater (calcium hydroxide solution) — if the limewater turns milky (cloudy white), carbon dioxide is confirmed.

Key Fact

The test for carbonates: add dilute acid → fizzing observed → gas turns limewater milky. The word equation is: carbonate + acid → salt + water + carbon dioxide. For example: CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2

Testing for Halide Ions

Halide ions — chloride (Cl¯), bromide (Br¯), and iodide (I¯) — are identified by adding dilute nitric acid followed by silver nitrate solution (AgNO3). The nitric acid is added first to remove any interfering carbonate or sulfite ions that could give false positives.

Chloride ions (Cl¯): Form a white precipitate of silver chloride (AgCl). Ag⁺ + Cl¯ → AgCl

Bromide ions (Br¯): Form a cream precipitate of silver bromide (AgBr). Ag⁺ + Br¯ → AgBr

Iodide ions (I¯): Form a yellow precipitate of silver iodide (AgI). Ag⁺ + I¯ → AgI

Testing for Sulfate Ions

Sulfate ions (SO4²¯) are identified by first adding dilute hydrochloric acid to remove any carbonate ions, then adding barium chloride solution (BaCl2). If sulfate ions are present, a white precipitate of barium sulfate (BaSO4) forms. The ionic equation is: Ba²⁺ + SO4²¯ → BaSO4

Key Fact

To test for sulfates: add dilute HCl, then barium chloride solution. A white precipitate of barium sulfate confirms sulfate ions are present. The HCl is added first to prevent false positives from carbonates.

Flame Emission Spectroscopy

Flame emission spectroscopy is an instrumental method of analysis that works on the same principle as flame tests but is far more accurate and sensitive. A sample is introduced into a flame, and the light emitted is passed through a spectroscope, which separates it into individual wavelengths. Each element produces a unique line spectrum — like a chemical fingerprint.

Sensitivity: Instrumental methods can detect very small quantities of an element — even trace amounts that chemical tests would miss. This makes them essential in forensic science, environmental monitoring, and quality control.

Speed and accuracy: Machines analyse samples much faster than manual chemical tests and produce quantitative results (exact concentrations), not just qualitative ones (present or absent). They are also more reliable because they remove the subjectivity of judging colours by eye.

Multiple elements: Flame emission spectroscopy can identify several different metal ions in a single sample. It can also measure their concentrations by comparing the intensity of emitted light against reference samples of known concentration.

Small sample size: Only a very small amount of sample is needed for analysis, which is useful when the sample is rare, expensive, or limited in quantity.

Cost: The equipment is expensive to buy and maintain. Specialist staff are needed to operate and calibrate the instruments.

Interpretation: Results must be interpreted using a database of reference spectra. Without this, raw data is meaningless. The instruments also need regular calibration against known standards to ensure accuracy.

Practical Tips for Ion Tests

When carrying out chemical tests for ions in a practical or answering exam questions about them, remember these key points. Always clean equipment between tests to avoid contamination. The order of reagent addition matters — adding nitric acid before silver nitrate for halides, and hydrochloric acid before barium chloride for sulfates. When describing observations, use precise colour terms: “white precipitate” rather than “it went white,” and “the limewater turned milky” rather than “it changed.”

A positively charged ion formed when a metal atom loses one or more electrons.
A negatively charged ion formed when a non-metal atom gains one or more electrons.
_____ Test Colours in Detail Lithium (Li¹⁺): Produces a crimson (deep red) flame
_____ (Na¹⁺): Produces a strong yellow flame

lessons.title: Materials, Corrosion, Haber Process and Fertilisers

before.content_html:
Corrosion

Corrosion is the destruction of a metal caused by reactions with substances in the environment. Most metals corrode when exposed to air and water over time. The most familiar example is the rusting of iron and steel.

Rusting is the corrosion of iron. It only happens when iron is in contact with both oxygen and water. The chemical name for rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide. Unlike the oxide layers on aluminium, rust is soft and flaky, so it falls away from the surface and exposes fresh metal underneath. This means rusting continues until all the iron has corroded.

Key Fact

Iron requires both oxygen and water to rust. Remove either one and rusting does not occur. This is the basis for all rust prevention methods.

Preventing Corrosion

Since rusting needs oxygen and water, prevention methods work by creating a barrier between the iron and these reactants, or by using a more reactive metal to protect the iron.

Painting: A layer of paint stops oxygen and water reaching the iron surface. Used on bridges, cars, and railings. If the paint is scratched or chips off, the iron underneath will rust.

Oiling or greasing: A thin coat of oil or grease creates a waterproof barrier. Used on moving parts such as bicycle chains and machine components, where paint would crack or wear off.

Electroplating: Coating the iron with a thin layer of another metal (such as tin, chromium, or nickel) using electrolysis. Tin cans are steel coated with tin. If the coating is breached, the iron underneath can still rust.

Galvanising: Coating iron or steel with a layer of zinc. Zinc acts as a barrier, but it also provides sacrificial protection — even if the coating is scratched, the zinc corrodes instead of the iron because zinc is more reactive.

Sacrificial protection uses a block of a more reactive metal (usually zinc or magnesium) attached to or near the iron structure. The more reactive metal oxidises preferentially, donating electrons to the iron and preventing it from reacting. This method is used on ships’ hulls, underground pipes, and offshore oil rigs. The sacrificial block must be replaced periodically as it is gradually consumed.

Alloys

An alloy is a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements (usually other metals, but sometimes non-metals like carbon). Alloys are made because pure metals are often too soft for practical use. In a pure metal, the atoms are arranged in regular layers that can slide over each other easily. In an alloy, atoms of different sizes disrupt the regular layers, making it harder for them to slide. This makes alloys harder and stronger than pure metals.

Key Fact

Most metals in everyday use are alloys, not pure metals. The different-sized atoms in an alloy disrupt the regular arrangement of layers, preventing them from sliding and making the alloy harder.

Steel is an alloy of iron and carbon (0.1–2% carbon). Low-carbon steel is easy to shape and used in car bodies. High-carbon steel is harder and used in cutting tools. Stainless steel contains chromium (and often nickel) and resists corrosion — used in cutlery, surgical instruments, and kitchen sinks.

Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin — hard and resistant to corrosion, used for statues and ship propellers. Brass is copper and zinc — harder than pure copper, used in musical instruments and plumbing fittings. Gold alloys are gold mixed with silver, copper, or zinc to make them harder — pure gold (24 carat) is too soft for jewellery.

Ceramics, Polymers, and Composites

Ceramics are non-metallic solids made by heating. Examples include clay pottery, bricks, and glass. Ceramics are very hard, resistant to heat and corrosion, but they are brittle — they shatter rather than bend when force is applied.

Composites are materials made by combining two or more different materials. Each component keeps its own properties, but together the composite has improved characteristics that neither material has alone. The two parts are a matrix (the background material that binds everything together) and a reinforcement (the material that adds strength or stiffness).

Concrete: Gravel or crusite (reinforcement) held together by cement (matrix). Strong in compression but weak in tension. Reinforced concrete: Steel bars or mesh (reinforcement) embedded in concrete (matrix) — strong in both compression and tension, used in buildings and bridges.

Fibreglass (GRP): Glass fibres (reinforcement) set in a polymer resin (matrix). Lightweight and strong, used in boat hulls, car body panels, and insulation. Carbon fibre reinforced polymer: Carbon fibres in a polymer resin. Extremely strong and lightweight, used in aircraft, racing cars, and tennis rackets.

The Haber Process

The Haber process is the industrial method for making ammonia (NH₃). Ammonia is a vital chemical because it is used to make fertilisers, nitric acid, and cleaning products. Without the Haber process, there would not be enough food to feed the world’s population.

The raw materials are nitrogen (obtained from the air by fractional distillation of liquid air) and hydrogen (obtained from natural gas or the cracking of hydrocarbons). The balanced equation is:

Key Fact

N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)

This reaction is reversible — it can go in both directions. The yield of ammonia is only about 15%, so unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled back through the reactor.

The conditions used in the Haber process represent a compromise between rate and yield:

Temperature: About 450 °C. The forward reaction is exothermic, so a lower temperature would give a higher yield. However, too low a temperature makes the reaction too slow. 450 °C is a compromise — fast enough to be economical, but the yield is only about 15%.

Pressure: About 200 atmospheres. There are 4 molecules of gas on the left (1 N₂ + 3 H₂) and only 2 on the right (2 NH₃). High pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with fewer gas molecules — the products. Higher pressures would give even higher yields, but they are expensive and dangerous.

Catalyst: An iron catalyst is used. It speeds up the reaction so equilibrium is reached faster. The catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium or the yield — it just helps the system get there more quickly.

The forward reaction is exothermic, so Le Chatelier’s principle says a lower temperature would shift equilibrium to the right and increase yield. But at low temperatures, the particles have less kinetic energy, fewer successful collisions occur, and the rate of reaction is too slow to be practical. The chosen temperature (450 °C) gives a reasonable rate with an acceptable yield. The unreacted gases are recycled to maximise overall conversion.

Similarly, very high pressures would increase yield further, but the cost of building and maintaining equipment that can withstand extreme pressures, along with increased safety risks, means 200 atmospheres is the economically practical compromise.

NPK Fertilisers

NPK fertilisers contain three essential elements that plants need for healthy growth:

Nitrogen (N) — promotes leaf and stem growth. Phosphorus (P) — promotes root development and helps with energy transfer. Potassium (K) — helps with disease resistance, flower and fruit development, and overall plant health.

Without these minerals, crops grow poorly. Intensive farming removes these elements from the soil faster than natural processes can replace them, so farmers add fertilisers to maintain crop yields and feed growing populations.

Key Fact

The nitrogen in NPK fertilisers comes from ammonia (via the Haber process). Ammonia can be reacted with nitric acid to produce ammonium nitrate (NH₄NO₃), a widely used nitrogen fertiliser. Phosphorus comes from phosphate rock, and potassium comes from potassium chloride or potassium sulfate mined from the ground.

In the laboratory, NPK fertilisers can be made by mixing the correct proportions of compounds containing nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. For example, mixing ammonium sulfate (provides N), potassium phosphate (provides P and K), and potassium chloride (provides K) in the right ratio produces a balanced NPK fertiliser. Industrially, ammonium nitrate is produced by neutralising ammonia solution with nitric acid: NH₃ + HNO₃ → NH₄NO₃.
